evals.name: object-page-great-wave
evals.prompt: Build the object page for Hokusai's Great Wave for the Edo unit of the F1 'Histories of making' course, as one self-contained HTML file (inline CSS, no build step). Use the image at /home/claude/creative-world/modules/F1-histories-of-making/build/units/edo/public/img/hi-wave.webp (copy it next to the HTML as hi-wave.webp and reference it relatively). Facts to use: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, JP1847, 'Under the Wave off Kanagawa (Kanagawa oki nami ura)', from Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, c. 1830–32, woodblock print, ink and colour on paper, 25.7 × 37.9 cm, CC0; publisher Nishimuraya Yohachi (Eijudō); the Met's spectroscopy found Prussian blue mixed with indigo in the dark stripes of the wave and pure Prussian blue, printed twice, in the hollow; the sky's pink was safflower and faded first; the title cartouche and the signature 'Hokusai aratame Iitsu hitsu' sit top left; three boats carry fish to Edo's market; Mount Fuji is small under the wave; about 8,000 impressions is the usual estimate (probable, Korenberg); 111 impressions located by 2020, 113 by 2024; no blocks survive. It needs: a left list of the nine world chapters with counts (F1.6 Africa 41, F1.7 The Americas 58, F1.8 East Asia 120, F1.9 South and Southeast Asia 44, F1.9a West Asia before Islam 37, F1.10 The Islamic world 66, F1.11 Europe and the Mediterranean 150, F1.12 Oceania 18, F1.12a The Arctic 9), the East Asia chapter expanded to its eight Edo lectures (L1 A city of a million, L2 Four hands one sheet, L3 Colour calendars poets, L4 The publisher, L5 Blue, L6 The ban and the road, L7 Afterlife, L8 Money); the globe in the middle with the route Berlin → Amsterdam → the Cape → Batavia → Nagasaki → Edo for the selected lecture and every other route dimmed; and a right panel for Lecture 5 with: the title, a one-line deck ('A European pigment's price curve, 1704–1831'), a paragraph (write 80–120 words from these facts: Prussian blue was made in Berlin around 1704 by accident; it reached Japan only through Nagasaki by Dutch ship; from 1824 Chinese junks undercut the Dutch and the Nagasaki price fell from 87 to 31 monme a kin by 1828; in 1829 an all-blue fan started a fad; at New Year 1831 Eijudō advertised Hokusai's Fuji series in the new blue), relations ('read in: F1.8 East Asia', 'shares routes with: F1.13 Networks', 'appears in: Act II, scenes 3–4'), two figures (1704–1831; 87 → 31 monme), sources (Smith, 'Prussian blue'; Fitzhugh; Korenberg), and previous / next (L4, L6). evals.name: seals-typology-and-eras-span-list
evals.prompt: Make one HTML page (inline CSS, self-contained) with two components for the Edo unit of the F1 'Histories of making' course. First, a typology plate of the censor's seals on Edo prints: four classes in rows: 'No seal required' 1600–1790; 'The kiwame seal 極' 1790–1843 (a round seal cut into the key block); 'Named censors' seals' 1843–1853 (one headman's name seal 1843–1847, then two from 1847); 'Aratame 改 and a date seal' 1853–1876 (a round aratame seal with a zodiac year-month date seal). Draw the seals as simple SVG marks (circles and squares with the characters 極, 改 and a placeholder name), one shelf per row, a date range under each seal, a note that the margin dates the sheet. Second, a span list of the six eras of the unit: A city is made 1603–1657; Black ink to colour 1657–1765; The golden age, under a censor 1765–1806; Blue and the road 1806–1842; The ban and the opening 1842–1868; The afterlife 1868–2024. The page should read as part of the course and work at 1440 px and 390 px; take screenshots at both widths with Playwright (require('/home/claude/creative-world/modules/F1-histories-of-making/build/lectures/node_modules/playwright'), executablePath '/opt/pw-browsers/chromium-1194/chrome-linux/chrome') and save them beside the HTML.
evals.expected_output: index.html + two screenshots; a typology plate and a span list in the course's finish

evals.name: grouping-page-arts-and-crafts
evals.prompt: Build the grouping page for the Arts and Crafts movement for the F1 'Histories of making' course, as one HTML file. Facts (from the course's canon, row MOV005): kind: movement; other name: Arts and Crafts; worlds F1.11 Europe, F1.7 the Americas, F1.13 Networks; sub-regions the British Isles, western and central Europe, the eastern United States; span 1860–1920, approximate; the name comes from the Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society, 1887; significance: it argued that the conditions of making (hand, workshop, pleasure in labour) mattered as much as the object, a claim later reworked by Mingei, Swadeshi and studio craft; materials and techniques: hand weaving, woodblock printing, natural dyeing, enamelling, letterpress; object types: wallpaper, textile, furniture, book, metalwork. Members to show as a gallery row (use grey placeholder frames with credit lines, no images needed): William Morris, 'Strawberry Thief' furnishing fabric, 1883, V&A T.586-1919 (documented); Morris & Co., 'Trellis' wallpaper, 1864, V&A E.452-1919 (documented); the Kelmscott Chaucer, 1896, Kelmscott Press (documented); Gustav Stickley, oak armchair, c. 1905–10, The Met (argued: American Craftsman is counted in by some historians and out by others); C. R. Ashbee, Guild of Handicraft silver dish, 1900 (documented). Neighbours and counterparts: the Aesthetic movement (1860s–1890s), Art Nouveau (1890–1910), Mingei (1925 – …), Swadeshi (1905 – …). What is argued: whether the movement was anti-industrial or a reform of industry (two readings, sources: Morris's 'The Lesser Arts' 1877; Ashbee's 'Craftsmanship in Competitive Industry' 1908); whether Morris's firm's socialist politics and its wealthy clientele contradict (two readings). What it leaves out: the women embroiderers of the Royal School of Art Needlework and the Morris firm's dye-works labourers, named in few records. Sources: Morris, 'The Lesser Arts' (1877); Ashbee (1908); V&A collection records; the Met collection record for the Stickley chair. The page should read as part of the course. Take a screenshot at 1440 × 900 (and a full-page one at 390 px wide where the page is meant to scroll) with Playwright (require('/home/claude/creative-world/modules/F1-histories-of-making/build/lectures/node_modules/playwright'), executablePath '/opt/pw-browsers/chromium-1194/chrome-linux/chrome') and save them beside the HTML as shot-1440.png and shot-390.png. Inline CSS, self-contained, no map libraries; schematic SVG where a map or a graph is needed. Google Fonts will not load in this sandbox; keep the links anyway.

evals.name: compare-sheet-tablet-khipu
evals.prompt: Build a comparison page for unit F1.1 'One object, three readings' of the F1 'Histories of making' course: a proto-cuneiform clay tablet recording barley (Uruk, c. 3100 BCE, The Met 1988.433.1, clay, 4.3 × 4.5 cm, CC0) beside an Inka khipu (Peru, c. 1400–1532, The Met 1994.35.129, cotton and camelid fibre, c. 60 cm, CC0), read through the same six readings: material (clay from the river plain, pressed with a reed stylus / spun cotton and camelid fibre, dyed), labour (a scribe trained in a temple household, unnamed / a khipukamayuq, a trained knot-keeper, unnamed), meaning (a count of barley rations owed to the temple, the sign for barley with number signs / a record whose decimal structure is understood but whose subject is not known for this khipu), trade (the barley came from temple fields, not traded / not known), technique (pressed and dried, not fired / knots of three kinds on pendant cords, position encodes value), use (kept in an archive, discarded once settled / carried by an official, read aloud; this one's use is not known). Every cell under 25 words with a claim id like c1, c2 in superscript; empty knowledge shown as 'not known'; a last row 'what this comparison leaves out' (that both records served states counting labour, and that neither names its maker); the two objects at one scale with the scale figure (a hand); credit lines; sources (the Met records; Nissen, Damerow and Englund, 'Archaic Bookkeeping' 1993; Urton, 'Signs of the Inka Khipu' 2003); previous / next. The page should read as part of the course. Take a screenshot at 1440 × 900 (and a full-page one at 390 px wide where the page is meant to scroll) with Playwright (require('/home/claude/creative-world/modules/F1-histories-of-making/build/lectures/node_modules/playwright'), executablePath '/opt/pw-browsers/chromium-1194/chrome-linux/chrome') and save them beside the HTML as shot-1440.png and shot-390.png. evals.name: living-practice-dine-weaving
evals.prompt: Build the Atlas page for Diné weaving as a living practice for unit F1.7 'The Americas, read through fibre' of the F1 'Histories of making' course, as one HTML file. The page must open with the community's protocol before any object: the community's own name first (Diné; the record: 'Navajo'); a Notice that attribution in older museum records is incomplete; a content note that some designs are not shown; a display-basis line for each object shown. Objects: a 'chief blanket', first phase, c. 1800–1850, The Met 1979.206.1227, wool, CC0, display basis 'made for trade; shown'; a Germantown 'eye-dazzler' blanket, c. 1880–90, The Met, wool, CC0, display basis 'made for sale; shown'; a sandpainting textile, 20th century, display basis 'not shown: ceremonial design; linked to the holder's record only' (draw a placeholder that says why, no image). Span: open-ended, 'c. 1650 – …' (documented from Spanish records of the 1600s; weaving continues today). Territory: Dinétah and the Navajo Nation, drawn as a soft wash on a schematic map, never a border line. What the record leaves out: the names of the weavers before the 1900s; the role of trading posts in setting designs. A review line: 'awaiting reader: Navajo Nation Museum' (do not invent a clearance). Sources: the Met collection records; Wheat, 'Blanket Weaving in the Southwest' 2003; Local Contexts TK Attribution Notice (text used exactly: 'This Notice is being used to correct historical practices of omission in attribution.'). Previous / next. The page should read as part of the course.
